laws.title: Kyoto Landscape Policy — Height Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Strict building height limits protect historic skyline
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's Landscape Policy (京都市景観計画, strengthened 2007) imposes among Japan's strictest height limits on new construction. In the historic districts surrounding Gion, Higashiyama, and Arashiyama, building heights are capped at 10–15 metres. Even central commercial areas (Kawaramachi, Karasuma) are capped at 31 metres. The policy also restricts signage colours and sizes. Several landmark buildings constructed before the 2007 tightening now exceed current limits and cannot be rebuilt as-is.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant construction: planning refusal; illegally built structures: demolition orders
exceptions: Pre-existing non-conforming buildings can be maintained but not expanded above the limit
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City Urban Planning Bureau — Landscape Policy

quiz.q: What is the maximum building height in Kyoto's most protected historic districts like Gion?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto's 2007 Landscape Policy caps buildings at 10–15 metres in its most protected historic districts — among Japan's strictest height limits.

laws.title: Outdoor Advertising Restriction Ordinance
laws.subtitle: Kyoto bans garish signs to protect historic aesthetic
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's Outdoor Advertising Ordinance (屋外広告物条例) is one of Japan's strictest, banning LED displays, neon signs, and oversized billboards in protected scenic zones. Even permitted signs must use earth tones and traditional colour palettes. In 2008, international chains including McDonald's and Lawson voluntarily adopted muted-colour branding for their Kyoto outlets. The ordinance distinguishes between preservation areas where signs are near-banned and general commercial zones.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant signs: removal orders + fines up to ¥300,000 per violation; repeat offences escalate
exceptions: Traffic and official government signs
Small shop name signs within approved dimensions

quiz.q: What did major chains like McDonald's do in Kyoto to comply with the Outdoor Advertising Ordinance?
options: Adopted muted, earth-tone branding instead of their standard colours
quiz.explanation: McDonald's, Lawson, and others voluntarily adopted muted earth-tone branding for Kyoto outlets to comply with the city's strict aesthetic preservation rules.

laws.title: Cultural Properties Protection — 17 UNESCO Sites
laws.subtitle: Kyoto has 17 UNESCO World Heritage properties
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's 17 UNESCO World Heritage properties — including Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion), Ryoan-ji, Nijo Castle, and Fushimi Inari Taisha — are protected under Japan's Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties (文化財保護法) and the World Heritage Convention. Any construction, development, or commercial activity near these sites requires cultural authority approval. Buffer zones around each site further restrict development. Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs oversees all national treasure designations.
laws.penalty: Damage to designated cultural property: up to 5 years imprisonment or ¥300,000 fine; development violations in buffer zones: planning refusal + demolition orders
exceptions: Approved restoration works by licensed heritage craftsmen
laws.sourceLabel: Agency for Cultural Affairs — World Heritage Kyoto

quiz.q: How many UNESCO World Heritage properties does Kyoto have?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto has 17 UNESCO World Heritage properties — more than any other Japanese city — including Kinkaku-ji, Nijo Castle, and Fushimi Inari Taisha.

laws.title: Gion Geiko District Photography Ordinance
laws.subtitle: Photographing geiko (geisha) in Gion without consent is banned
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's Gion district (祇園) enacted Japan's first local ordinance banning unwanted photography of geiko (芸妓) and maiko (舞妓) in public streets in March 2019. The ordinance — Kyoto City Gion District Tourism Management Ordinance — covers the historic stone-paved Hanamikoji-dori and surrounding streets. Tourists who harass or photograph geiko without consent face fines. The move came after incidents of tourists grabbing geiko for photos and obstructing their movement.
laws.penalty: Photographing geiko/maiko without consent in Gion: ¥10,000 fine; physical harassment: criminal assault charges
exceptions: Photography within licensed ozashiki (geisha banquet) contexts with host permission
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City — Gion Tourism Management Ordinance

quiz.q: What triggered Kyoto's 2019 ordinance banning photography of geiko in Gion?
options: Tourists grabbing and harassing geiko for photos
quiz.explanation: Incidents of tourists physically grabbing geiko and maiko to pose for photos — disrupting their work routes — prompted Kyoto's pioneering anti-harassment photography ordinance.

laws.title: Overtourism Management Regulations
laws.subtitle: Kyoto managing 50+ million annual visitor impacts
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto received over 50 million tourists in 2019, straining infrastructure and resident quality of life. The city has implemented area-specific visitor management: Arashiyama's bamboo grove limits crowds through timed entry pilots, certain Geisha districts restrict pedestrian access during peak hours, and the Philosopher's Walk (哲学の道) has conduct guidelines. A tourist tax (宿泊税) of ¥200–¥1,000 per night was introduced in 2018 to fund management measures.
laws.penalty: Visitor conduct violations in restricted zones: fines up to ¥50,000; entering closed areas: trespass charges
exceptions: Residents and delivery workers retain access to restricted zones

quiz.q: What accommodation tax did Kyoto introduce in 2018 to fund tourism management?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto's 2018 accommodation tax charges ¥200–¥1,000 per night depending on the room rate — used to fund tourism management and infrastructure.

laws.title: Kyoto Bus Congestion Management
laws.subtitle: Tourist buses restricted from central historic routes
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City has progressively restricted tourist bus access to central areas. Large tour buses cannot park along Shijo-dori and Kawaramachi-dori during peak hours. A designated coach terminal at Hachijo-guchi (near Kyoto Station) serves as the required coach drop-off point. Private car access to Arashiyama and Higashiyama during peak season is restricted under the Road Traffic Act's traffic restriction provisions. City buses operate priority lanes.
laws.penalty: Illegal bus parking in restricted zones: ¥18,000 fine; operating outside designated routes: administrative penalty
exceptions: Resident and service vehicles with ward permits

quiz.q: Where must large tourist coaches drop off passengers in central Kyoto?
options: Designated coach terminal at Hachijo-guchi near Kyoto Station
quiz.explanation: Kyoto requires large tourist coaches to use the Hachijo-guchi terminal near Kyoto Station rather than accessing historic centre streets.

laws.title: Kyoto Protocol Legacy — Local Carbon Targets
laws.subtitle: Kyoto city maintains ambitious carbon reduction goals
laws.fullDescription: The Kyoto Protocol (京都議定書), signed in Kyoto in 1997, set binding emissions reduction targets for developed nations. While the Protocol was a national/international instrument, Kyoto City itself has committed to 70% CO2 reduction from 1990 levels by 2050, exceeding national targets. The city's Low-Carbon City Promotion Plan includes solar panel subsidies, district heating networks, and restrictions on new fossil-fuel heating systems in city facilities.
laws.penalty: City facilities non-compliant with energy standards: internal administrative measures; private sector: standard emissions reporting requirements
exceptions: Heritage buildings exempt from some energy retrofit mandates if structural integrity would be compromised
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City — Low Carbon City Promotion Plan

quiz.q: In what year was the Kyoto Protocol signed in Kyoto city?
quiz.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol — the first binding international climate treaty — was signed in Kyoto, Japan in December 1997.

laws.title: Kinkaku-ji Arson Law
laws.subtitle: Japan's famous arson case shaped cultural property law
laws.fullDescription: The 1950 arson of Kinkaku-ji (the Golden Pavilion) by a young monk — immortalised in Mishima Yukio's novel 'The Temple of the Golden Pavilion' — directly prompted strengthening of Japan's cultural property protection laws. The 1950 Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties (文化財保護法) was enacted partly in response. The rebuilt Kinkaku-ji (1955) is now designated a Special Historical Site and World Cultural Heritage property. Any damage to it carries maximum heritage penalty provisions.
laws.penalty: Damage to National Treasure or Special Historic Site: up to 5 years imprisonment + full restoration cost civil liability
laws.sourceLabel: Agency for Cultural Affairs — Cultural Properties Protection Law 1950

quiz.q: What event directly prompted Japan to enact the 1950 Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties?
options: WWII bombing damage to Nara temples
Arson of Kinkaku-ji by a young monk
Flood damage to Kyoto's canal network
quiz.explanation: The 1950 arson of Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion) by a novice monk prompted Japan to enact comprehensive cultural properties protection legislation.

laws.title: Kyoto Smoking Ban — Preservation Zone Extension
laws.subtitle: Smoking banned across all heritage district streets
laws.fullDescription: Beyond the national 2020 indoor smoking ban, Kyoto City extends a near-total outdoor smoking ban to all designated Historic Preservation Areas (歴史的景観保全地区). This covers Gion, Higashiyama, Arashiyama, Nishiki, and over 50 designated zones. Smoking is prohibited while walking anywhere in these areas. Designated smoking areas (指定喫煙所) are scarce — usually only near major transport hubs. The restriction aims to prevent fire risk to wooden historic structures.
laws.penalty: Smoking in prohibited outdoor zones: ¥1,000 fine (on-the-spot); area enforcement officers patrol peak season
exceptions: Designated smoking areas (指定喫煙所) clearly marked
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City — Smoking Regulation in Historic Districts

quiz.q: Why does Kyoto extend its outdoor smoking ban to historic district streets beyond the national rules?
options: Fire risk to wooden historic structures
quiz.explanation: Kyoto's outdoor smoking ban in historic areas primarily addresses fire risk — the densely packed wooden buildings of Gion and Higashiyama are extremely vulnerable.

laws.title: Machiya Traditional Town House Preservation
laws.subtitle: Kyoto subsidises preservation of wooden townhouses
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's Machiya Regeneration Programme (町家再生プログラム) provides subsidies and low-interest loans for owners of traditional wooden townhouses (町家) to restore rather than demolish them. At their 1990 peak, 28,000 machiya existed in Kyoto; by 2022 fewer than 22,000 remained due to demolitions. A 2008 ordinance requires owners to notify the city before demolishing a machiya over 50 years old — creating a 6-month window for the city to propose preservation alternatives.
laws.penalty: Demolishing without notification: fines up to ¥300,000; demolishing a designated preservation machiya: restoration orders
exceptions: Structurally unsafe buildings may be demolished urgently with post-notification

quiz.q: How many traditional machiya townhouses remain in Kyoto as of 2022 (down from 28,000)?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto's machiya population declined from ~28,000 in 1990 to fewer than 22,000 by 2022 — despite preservation programmes — due to demolitions for modern development.

laws.title: Kyoto Bicycle Parking Rules
laws.subtitle: Illegal bicycle parking removed in historic tourist zones
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City's bicycle parking ordinance bans locking bicycles to railings, street furniture, and gates in designated management zones — particularly around Kyoto Station, Nishiki Market, and shrine/temple approaches. Illegally parked bicycles are removed to a bicycle pound (自転車保管所) and owners must pay a retrieval fee. The city operates over 30 designated bicycle parking facilities. Designated free bicycle parking is available near major attractions during peak season.
laws.penalty: Illegally parked bicycle removal fee: ¥2,300 retrieval + ¥500/day storage; unclaimed after 3 months: destroyed or recycled
exceptions: Registered bicycles with disabled parking permits
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City Transportation Bureau — Bicycle Parking

quiz.q: What happens to illegally parked bicycles in Kyoto's designated management zones?
options: A fine notice is attached but bicycle is left
Bicycle is removed to a pound; owner pays retrieval fee
quiz.explanation: Illegally parked bicycles in Kyoto's management zones are removed to a pound — owners pay a ¥2,300 retrieval fee plus daily storage charges.

laws.title: Kyoto Regional Minimum Wage
laws.subtitle: Kyoto's minimum wage higher than national average
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto Prefecture's regional minimum wage as of October 2024 stands at ¥1,077 per hour — above the national weighted average. Kyoto's economy is heavily reliant on tourism, traditional crafts (Nishijin-ori weaving, Kiyomizu pottery), and high-tech manufacturing (Kyocera, Shimadzu, Murata are all Kyoto-headquartered companies). The blend of artisan, service, and high-tech employment creates diverse minimum wage compliance needs.
laws.penalty: Employers paying below minimum: fines up to ¥500,000
exceptions: Apprenticeship exceptions require Labour Bureau approval

quiz.q: Which major electronics company — maker of capacitors and sensors — is headquartered in Kyoto?
quiz.explanation: Murata Manufacturing — the world's largest capacitor producer — is headquartered in Kyoto, part of the city's significant high-tech manufacturing sector.

laws.title: Traditional Craft Industry Protection
laws.subtitle: Nishijin weaving and Kiyomizu ware designated traditional crafts
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Act on the Promotion of Traditional Craft Industries (伝統的工芸品産業の振興に関する法律) designates protected traditional industries whose products must meet strict production criteria — primarily handmade, using traditional techniques and materials. Kyoto has 17 designated traditional crafts including Nishijin-ori (西陣織) silk weaving, Kyoto Nishiki (京友禅) dyed textiles, and Kiyomizu-yaki (清水焼) pottery. Fake 'Nishijin-ori' products without the official certificate violate the Act.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent use of traditional craft designations: up to 1 year imprisonment or ¥1,000,000 fine
exceptions: Products using traditional techniques but produced outside strict geographic criteria may be sold without the designation mark
laws.sourceLabel: METI — Traditional Craft Industries Promotion Act

quiz.q: What is Nishijin-ori (西陣織) — one of Kyoto's most famous traditional crafts?
quiz.explanation: Nishijin-ori (西陣織) is Kyoto's famous hand-woven silk textile craft — produced in the Nishijin district since the 5th century and protected as a designated traditional craft.

laws.title: Gion Matsuri Road Closure Rules
laws.subtitle: Annual festival requires major traffic management
laws.fullDescription: The Gion Matsuri (祇園祭), held throughout July and one of Japan's three greatest festivals, involves elaborate float processions (山鉾巡行) that require closure of central Kyoto streets. Under the Road Traffic Act, the Kyoto Prefectural Police issues temporary road use permits and establishes crowd control zones. Roping off streets, prohibiting private vehicles, and directing pedestrian flow are mandatory. The festival's yamaboko floats are UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.
laws.penalty: Entering closed vehicle zones during procession: traffic offence + fines; damaging floats: criminal property damage
exceptions: Emergency vehicles retain access with police escort

quiz.q: What UNESCO status do the yamaboko floats of the Gion Matsuri hold?
quiz.explanation: The Gion Matsuri's yamaboko float processions are inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list, recognising them as living cultural traditions.

laws.title: Satoyama Landscape Preservation
laws.subtitle: Traditional rural landscape around Kyoto protected
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto Prefecture's satoyama (里山) — traditional semi-natural landscapes of bamboo groves, mixed forests, and rice paddies on the city's outskirts (Arashiyama, Ohara, Kurama) — are protected under the Natural Environment Preservation Act and Kyoto's own Green Vision Plan. Bamboo, an invasive species if unmanaged, is subject to mandatory control in designated zones. Development in satoyama zones requires environmental impact assessment.
laws.penalty: Unauthorised development in satoyama preservation zones: administrative orders + fines up to ¥500,000
exceptions: Traditional agricultural activities including bamboo harvesting are encouraged, not restricted

quiz.q: What does 'satoyama' (里山) refer to in Japanese environmental policy?
options: Traditional semi-natural rural landscapes between settlements and mountains
quiz.explanation: Satoyama (里山) refers to Japan's traditional patchwork landscapes of bamboo groves, mixed forests, and farmland that buffer between human settlements and mountains.

laws.title: Kyoto City Bond — Cultural Preservation Financing
laws.subtitle: Kyoto issues cultural preservation bonds
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City issues municipal bonds (京都市債) under the Local Finance Law to fund cultural preservation works, temple approach road repairs, and infrastructure maintenance near UNESCO sites. The city's fiscal position has been challenged by high maintenance costs for heritage infrastructure — the cost of repairing Kyoto's historic road networks alone exceeds ¥10 billion annually. Bond issuance requires Ministry of Internal Affairs approval given Kyoto's debt levels.
laws.penalty: N/A — municipal finance instrument; default on bonds subject to national government intervention
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City Finance Bureau — Municipal Bonds

quiz.q: Approximately how much does Kyoto City spend annually just on historic road network maintenance near heritage sites?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto's historic road repair and heritage infrastructure maintenance costs exceed ¥10 billion annually — a significant fiscal burden driving municipal bond issuance.

laws.title: Cannabis Prohibition — Kyoto University Context
laws.subtitle: Japan's cannabis laws apply equally to students
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto University (京都大学), Japan's second most prestigious institution, has experienced periodic cannabis arrests among students. Japan's Cannabis Control Act applies equally to students — no academic exemption exists. Kyoto Prefectural Police narcotics division actively investigates student drug use networks. Since 2022, Japanese law allows cannabis-derived medicines (CBD products remain in a grey zone — cannabidiol with no THC is not explicitly regulated).
laws.penalty: Cannabis possession: up to 5 years imprisonment; cultivation/import: up to 7 years; arrest typically followed by expulsion from university
exceptions: Licensed hemp producers; approved cannabis medicines from 2024

quiz.q: What is Japan's second most prestigious national university, located in Kyoto?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto University (京都大学, Kyodai) is Japan's second most prestigious national university after the University of Tokyo — producing 10 Nobel laureates.

laws.title: Kyoto Tram Heritage — Eizan Railway
laws.subtitle: Historic narrow-gauge railways operate under Railway Act
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto retains several historic narrow-gauge and heritage railways: the Eizan Electric Railway (叡山電鉄) serving the northern Demachiyanagi–Kibune/Kurama corridor and the Keifuku Electric Railway (嵐電, Randen) tram serving Arashiyama. These operate under the Railway Business Act (鉄道事業法). The Randen — running through residential streets in west Kyoto — has a 6km/h speed limit at pedestrian crossings. Both railways are tourist attractions subject to non-photography zones at scenic points.
laws.penalty: Fare evasion: surcharges; trespassing on tracks: criminal trespass + fines
exceptions: Emergency maintenance crews

quiz.q: What is the colloquial name for Kyoto's Keifuku Electric Railway — a beloved historic tram?
quiz.explanation: Keifuku Electric Railway is affectionately called Randen (嵐電) — a charming historic tram running through Kyoto's residential streets to Arashiyama.

laws.title: Geiko Licensing and Training System
laws.subtitle: Geiko profession governed by Gion Kobu Kabukai
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's geiko (芸妓) and maiko (舞妓) — professional traditional entertainers of the five hanamachi (花街) districts — are trained and licenced by the Gion Kobu Kabukai and equivalent bodies. While not government-regulated per se, the hanamachi system intersects with employment law (geiko are typically independent contractors or employees of okiya (置屋)), working hours, and the minimum age for maiko (officially 15, debated due to labour law). The okiya must register with Kyoto City.
laws.penalty: Labour law violations in the hanamachi: standard employment law penalties; minors working outside permitted hours: up to ¥300,000 fine for operators
exceptions: Cultural performance exemptions for traditional arts apply but are limited

quiz.q: What is a 'hanamachi' (花街) in Kyoto?
quiz.explanation: A hanamachi (花街, 'flower town') is a geisha entertainment district — Kyoto has five, including the most famous Gion Kobu.

laws.title: Uji Matcha Geographical Indication
laws.subtitle: Authentic Uji matcha protected by GI certification
laws.fullDescription: Uji City (宇治市) in Kyoto Prefecture is Japan's most famous tea-producing region. 'Uji Tea' (宇治茶) is protected by Japan's Geographical Indication (GI) system under the Act for Protection of Specified Agricultural, Forestry, Fishery and Food Products. Products must meet origin and production method criteria to bear the Uji Tea GI mark. The Kyoto GI system has expanded to cover Kyoto vegetables (京野菜) and certain traditional craft products.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent use of Uji Tea or Kyoto GI marks: up to 1 year imprisonment or ¥1,000,000 fine
exceptions: Generic tea product descriptions ('Uji-style') without the official GI mark are not violations
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Agriculture — Geographical Indication System

quiz.q: What type of legal protection covers 'Uji Tea' to prevent counterfeit products?
quiz.explanation: Uji Tea is protected by Japan's Geographical Indication (GI) system — only tea meeting origin and production criteria can be labelled with the official GI mark.

laws.title: Deer and Wildlife in Kyoto Outskirts
laws.subtitle: Wildlife management as deer expand from Nara
laws.fullDescription: As Nara's sika deer (鹿) population expands north into Kyoto Prefecture (Kurama, Kibune areas), Kyoto has implemented wildlife management permits under the Wildlife Protection and Hunting Act (鳥獣保護管理法). Deer damage to Satoyama vegetation and temple gardens is a growing problem. Kyoto Prefecture issues culling permits while also encouraging eco-tourism deer viewing. Feeding deer outside designated areas is prohibited to prevent habituation.
laws.penalty: Illegal deer feeding in prohibited zones: ¥50,000 fine; unlicensed deer hunting: up to 1 year imprisonment or ¥1,000,000 fine
exceptions: Licensed hunters during designated season
Farmers protecting crops under damage prevention permits

quiz.q: From which famous Japanese city is the sika deer population expanding northward into Kyoto's forests?
quiz.explanation: Nara's famous free-roaming sika deer population is expanding, with deer increasingly appearing in Kyoto's northern Kurama and Kibune mountain areas.

laws.title: Shrine and Temple Entry Regulations
laws.subtitle: Trespassing on sacred grounds strictly enforced
laws.fullDescription: Many of Kyoto's shrines and temples (神社・寺院) close at night and restrict entry to ticket-holding visitors. Trespassing in closed sacred sites — a growing problem with social media-driven visitors seeking dawn or night photos — is prosecuted under criminal trespass provisions (不法侵入, Penal Code Article 130). The monks and priests managing these properties have been vocal about nighttime intrusions. Kinkaku-ji and Fushimi Inari have security patrols.
laws.penalty: Trespassing in closed shrine/temple: up to 3 years imprisonment or ¥100,000 fine; damage to sacred objects: up to 5 years
exceptions: Authorised pre-dawn photography sessions booked through official channels
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City — Cultural Properties Protection Office

quiz.q: What drives the growing problem of nighttime trespassing at Kyoto's shrines and temples?
options: Social media influencers seeking exclusive dawn/night photos
quiz.explanation: Social media pressure to capture unique dawn or closed-hours photos has driven a sharp rise in trespassing at Kyoto's sacred sites.

laws.title: Kyoto High-Tech Industry Tax Incentives
laws.subtitle: Kyoto Prefecture supports semiconductor and biotech firms
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto Prefecture operates the Kyoto Industrial Location Incentive System providing tax reductions (fixed asset tax reduction up to 100% for 5 years) and infrastructure grants for companies establishing advanced manufacturing in designated industrial zones. Target industries include semiconductors (Rohm, Kyocera), measurement instruments (Shimadzu, Horiba), and pharmaceuticals. The scheme operates under the Act on Temporary Measures for the Promotion of Business Location in Specified Areas.
laws.penalty: Companies misusing incentives (moving before commitment period ends): clawback of all benefits
exceptions: Biotech and green energy companies receive extended incentive periods

quiz.q: Which famous scientific instrument company, maker of mass spectrometers, is headquartered in Kyoto?
quiz.explanation: Shimadzu Corporation — maker of analytical instruments, medical equipment, and mass spectrometers — has been headquartered in Kyoto since 1875.

laws.title: Kyoto Prefectural Assembly Electoral District
laws.subtitle: Kyoto's electoral system under national rules
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto Prefecture elects members to the national House of Representatives (衆議院) from 6 electoral districts under the Public Offices Election Act. Kyoto City Council (48 seats) and Prefectural Assembly (60 seats) are separately elected. Kyoto's student population (approximately 135,000 students — Japan's highest student-to-resident ratio) creates an unusual electorate. Voter registration can be at university address, benefiting student participation.
laws.penalty: Vote buying: up to 3 years imprisonment; electoral fraud: disqualification
exceptions: Non-citizens cannot vote in national or prefectural elections
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Internal Affairs — Kyoto Electoral Districts

quiz.q: What makes Kyoto's electorate unusual compared to other Japanese prefectural capitals?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto has Japan's highest student-to-resident ratio — approximately 135,000 university students among a city population of ~1.4 million — creating a distinctively young electorate.

laws.title: Kyoto Noh Theatre and Performance Licensing
laws.subtitle: Noh theatre registered as UNESCO Intangible Heritage
laws.fullDescription: Noh (能) theatre, originating in Kyoto in the 14th century under Zeami Motokiyo and patronised by the Muromachi Shogunate, is registered as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage. Kyoto's Kanze Noh Theatre (観世流宗家) is the headquarters of the largest Noh school. Noh performers must study for 10–20 years under licensed masters. While not regulated by government licensing, the Noh Association (社団法人能楽協会) controls certification, and performances use cultural property instruments subject to preservation rules.
laws.penalty: Damage to Noh cultural property instruments (National Treasure category): up to 5 years + restoration

quiz.q: Who developed Noh theatre in 14th century Kyoto, codifying it as a high art form?
quiz.explanation: Zeami Motokiyo (世阿弥元清) developed and codified Noh theatre in 14th century Kyoto — writing 200+ plays and essential acting theory texts still used today.

laws.title: Kyoto Vegetarian/Buddhist Dietary Practices
laws.subtitle: Shojin ryori temple cuisine subject to food standards
laws.fullDescription: Shojin ryori (精進料理) — Zen Buddhist vegan temple cuisine — is a Kyoto culinary tradition with legal implications for restaurant labelling. Under the Food Labelling Act, restaurants serving shojin ryori must accurately label if any non-vegan ingredients are used. Growing inbound tourism demand for genuine vegan and halal options has led Kyoto City to issue restaurant guidance on allergen and dietary disclosure. Over 100 Kyoto restaurants are registered on the city's halal/vegan-friendly database.
laws.penalty: Mislabelling of vegan or religious dietary foods: civil liability for health impacts; criminal fraud if deliberate (up to 2 years)
exceptions: Traditional temple kitchens on enclosed religious properties
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City Tourism Promotion Division — Dietary Information

quiz.q: What is 'shojin ryori' (精進料理)?
quiz.explanation: Shojin ryori (精進料理) is the vegan Buddhist temple cuisine of Japan — a Kyoto tradition dating from Zen monasteries, now served at many temple restaurants.

laws.title: Kamo River Management Ordinance
laws.subtitle: Kyoto's iconic river subject to strict bank use rules
laws.fullDescription: The Kamo River (鴨川), flowing through central Kyoto, is subject to the Kamo River Ordinance (鴨川条例) which governs its banks. The famous kawayuka (川床) — wooden decks extending over the river from restaurants along Pontocho — are licensed annually by Kyoto City and must comply with precise placement, load, and drainage standards. Bathing, fishing with hooks (net fishing permitted with permit), and driving vehicles onto river beds are prohibited.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed kawayuka deck: removal orders + fines up to ¥500,000; prohibited river activities: fines up to ¥50,000
exceptions: Licensed seasonal kawayuka with annual permit
Traditional cormorant fishing (鵜飼) with permission

quiz.q: What are 'kawayuka' (川床) — Kyoto's famous seasonal riverside structures?
options: Floating lanterns set on the river
Licensed wooden dining decks extending over the Kamo River from riverside restaurants
Stone stepping stones crossing the river
quiz.explanation: Kawayuka (川床) are the famous licensed wooden dining platforms that Pontocho district restaurants extend over the Kamo River during summer — a quintessential Kyoto experience.

laws.title: Kyoto as Japan's Academic Capital
laws.subtitle: Densest concentration of universities in Japan
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto Prefecture has over 30 universities and colleges — the highest concentration per capita in Japan. National universities include Kyoto University (iPS cell research, 10 Nobel laureates) and Kyoto Institute of Technology. Private institutions include Doshisha, Ritsumeikan, and Kyoto Sangyo. The University Act (学校教育法) governs all accreditation. Kyoto University's unconventional culture (students historically resisted entrance exams with 'academic freedom' protests) is protected by academic freedom provisions.
laws.penalty: Unaccredited institutions claiming university status: up to ¥1,000,000 fine + closure
exceptions: Research institutes affiliated with accredited universities can use academic titles

quiz.q: What Nobel Prize-winning research is particularly associated with Kyoto University?
options: Medicine (iPS cell development by Shinya Yamanaka)
quiz.explanation: Kyoto University's Shinya Yamanaka won the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for developing induced pluripotent stem cells (iPS cells) — a landmark Kyoto discovery.

laws.title: Fushimi Inari Visitor Safety Rules
laws.subtitle: Mountain trail management at Japan's most visited shrine
laws.fullDescription: Fushimi Inari Taisha (伏見稲荷大社) — Japan's most visited shrine, with over 10,000 vermilion torii gates ascending Mt. Inari — has implemented visitor safety rules for the 4km mountain trail. The shrine is open 24 hours but the upper mountain becomes dangerous at night. Staff and volunteer guides patrol the lower trails. Theft of torii offerings, graffiti on torii gates, and leaving rubbish on the mountain path are criminal acts. The shrine privately owns the mountain.
laws.penalty: Graffiti on torii: criminal property damage up to 3 years + restoration cost; theft of offerings: up to 10 years

quiz.q: Approximately how many vermilion torii gates line the trails of Fushimi Inari Taisha?
quiz.explanation: Fushimi Inari Taisha has approximately 10,000 vermilion torii gates donated by individuals and businesses — forming the iconic tunnel-like path up Mt. Inari.

laws.title: Traditional Inn (Ryokan) Standards
laws.subtitle: Ryokan licensed under Hotel Business Act with specific rules
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's approximately 800 ryokan (traditional inns) are licensed under the Hotel Business Act (旅館業法) as a separate category from western hotels. Ryokan must meet specific room size, bathing facility, and service standards. As traditional establishments, many have age-old operational customs (check-in times, communal bath etiquette, kaiseki dinner procedures) that have partial codification in their operating licences. Ryokan rates are unregulated (unlike the postwar price control era).
laws.penalty: Operating ryokan without licence: up to 6 months imprisonment or ¥1,000,000 fine; hygiene violations: closure orders
exceptions: Minpaku (Airbnb) properties cannot use ryokan designation — separate licensing required
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health — Hotel Business Act (Ryokan)

quiz.q: Approximately how many traditional ryokan operate in Kyoto city?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto has approximately 800 licensed ryokan — one of Japan's highest concentrations — serving domestic and international guests seeking traditional accommodation experiences.

laws.title: Kyoto Animation Memorial Site Rules
laws.subtitle: Restrictions on filming near tragedy memorial
laws.fullDescription: The Kyoto Animation arson attack (July 2019, 36 killed) was Japan's deadliest mass murder since WWII. The studio site in Fushimi Ward has become a memorial location. Kyoto Animation and city authorities have issued guidance asking visitors not to film or post content that could identify victims' memorials or film inside the rebuilding studio. Privacy laws (Personal Information Protection Act) cover any footage identifying individuals. The perpetrator was convicted and sentenced to death in 2024.
laws.penalty: Filming inside active studio without consent: criminal trespass; exploitative content using victims' likenesses: civil tort
exceptions: Officially sanctioned memorial photography

quiz.q: How many people were killed in the 2019 Kyoto Animation arson attack?
quiz.explanation: The 2019 Kyoto Animation arson killed 36 people — Japan's deadliest mass murder since WWII and a national tragedy for the anime industry.

laws.title: Tea Ceremony Cultural Property
laws.subtitle: Sen no Rikyu's tea houses are National Treasures
laws.fullDescription: The Japanese tea ceremony (茶道, chado) was codified in Kyoto by Sen no Rikyu in the 16th century. Historic tea houses (茶室) associated with Rikyu's tradition — including Taian at Yamazaki and properties of the Urasenke and Omotesenke schools in Kyoto — are designated National Treasures or Important Cultural Properties. Tea utensils (茶器) of historical significance are similarly protected. The three Kyoto Sen family schools collectively train over 1 million practitioners.
laws.penalty: Damage to National Treasure tea house or utensil: up to 5 years imprisonment + restoration
exceptions: Normal use by licensed practitioners in approved ceremonies

quiz.q: Who codified the Japanese tea ceremony (茶道) in 16th century Kyoto, becoming its most revered master?
quiz.explanation: Sen no Rikyu (千利休) codified the Japanese tea ceremony in 16th century Kyoto — his wabi-sabi aesthetic principles remain the foundation of all major tea schools.

laws.title: Disaster Resilience Retrofitting — Kyoto
laws.subtitle: Pre-1981 buildings in historic districts must be assessed
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's high proportion of pre-1981 wooden buildings (both historic machiya and postwar construction) creates significant earthquake vulnerability. Under the Building Standards Act and Kyoto City's own Seismic Assessment Programme, buildings with four or more floors built before 1981 must undergo assessment. The city offers subsidies (up to 23% of retrofit costs for heritage structures). Seismically deficient buildings on Kyoto's listed high-risk streets face mandatory assessment orders.
laws.penalty: Failure to comply with mandatory assessment order for flagged buildings: public notification; persistent refusal: administrative orders
exceptions: Buildings with current structural survey confirming compliance

quiz.q: What percentage of retrofit costs does Kyoto City subsidise for heritage structures undergoing earthquake strengthening?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto City subsidises up to 23% of earthquake retrofit costs for designated heritage structures — incentivising owners to strengthen machiya and other historic buildings.

laws.title: Nishiki Market Vendor Fraud Prevention
laws.subtitle: Tourist-area pricing must comply with consumer law
laws.fullDescription: Nishiki Market (錦市場), Kyoto's historic covered food market, has seen rising tourist prices for traditional foods. While price-setting is generally free, deceptive pricing practices (displaying a false 'original price', denying refunds required under the Specified Commercial Transactions Act, or mislabelling food origin) are subject to Consumer Affairs Agency and Kyoto City enforcement. Several vendors have received administrative guidance for deceptive tourist pricing.
laws.penalty: Deceptive pricing: cease-and-desist; persistent violations: fines up to 3% of related sales; food fraud: up to 2 years
exceptions: Premium pricing for high-quality ingredients is fully legal
laws.sourceLabel: Consumer Affairs Agency — Price Representation Rules

quiz.q: What is Kyoto's Nishiki Market (錦市場) commonly nicknamed?
quiz.explanation: Nishiki Market is nicknamed 'Kyoto's Kitchen' (京の台所) — a 400-year-old covered market in central Kyoto selling fresh produce, pickles, and traditional food.

laws.title: Bamboo Grove Protection — Arashiyama
laws.subtitle: Arashiyama bamboo grove under strict conduct rules
laws.fullDescription: The Arashiyama bamboo grove (竹林の小径) is Kyoto's most photographed natural landscape. The bamboo is private property owned largely by Jojakko-ji temple and managed under cooperation with Kyoto City. Rules prohibit: touching or cutting bamboo, leaving rubbish, cycling within the grove, and extended photography sessions that block the path. The grove is open 24 hours but nighttime access is informally discouraged after light-up events conclude. Peak morning hours before 8am remain the least crowded.
laws.penalty: Cutting or damaging bamboo: property damage charge; cycling in prohibited zone: ¥5,000 fine
exceptions: Official photography sessions with landowner and city permission

quiz.q: Who primarily owns the famous Arashiyama bamboo grove's land in Kyoto?
options: Jojakko-ji temple and adjacent private landowners
quiz.explanation: The Arashiyama bamboo grove path runs largely through Jojakko-ji temple land and adjacent private properties — managed in cooperation with Kyoto City.

laws.title: Art and Antique Export Control
laws.subtitle: Cultural property export requires Agency approval
laws.fullDescription: Under the Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties, export of designated cultural properties from Japan — including antique ceramics, Buddhist art, tea utensils, and historical documents — requires approval from the Commissioner for Cultural Affairs. Kyoto's antique districts (Shinmonzen and Furumonzen streets) deal in significant pieces that approach or meet export control thresholds. Japan Customs maintains a list of culturally sensitive items requiring pre-export screening.
laws.penalty: Exporting controlled cultural property without approval: up to 5 years imprisonment or ¥5,000,000 fine
exceptions: Temporary export for museum exhibitions with return guarantee
laws.sourceLabel: Agency for Cultural Affairs — Export Control

quiz.q: Which Kyoto streets are famous for antique dealers specialising in Japanese art and cultural objects?
quiz.explanation: Shinmonzen (新門前通) and Furumonzen (古門前通) are Kyoto's premier antique dealer streets — a global destination for Japanese ceramics, lacquerware, and Buddhist art.

laws.title: Medical Tourism and Dental Treatment Rules
laws.subtitle: Foreign patients must use licensed practitioners
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto has seen growth in medical tourism, particularly for dental work, cosmetic procedures, and traditional medicine (kampo 漢方). All medical and dental practitioners must hold Japanese government licences under the Medical Practitioners Act (医師法) and Dental Practitioners Act (歯科医師法). Kampo (traditional Chinese/Japanese medicine) prescribed by licenced doctors is covered by national health insurance. Unlicensed practitioners offering medical services to foreign visitors have been prosecuted.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed medical practice: up to 3 years imprisonment or ¥1,000,000 fine
exceptions: Licensed practitioners holding foreign credentials in limited exchange agreements
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health — Medical Practitioners Act

quiz.q: What traditional medical system — combining Chinese and Japanese herbal medicine — is covered by Japan's national health insurance?
options: Kampo (漢方, traditional Japanese-Chinese herbal medicine)
quiz.explanation: Kampo (漢方) — Japan's traditional herbal medicine system derived from Chinese medicine — is covered by national health insurance when prescribed by a licensed doctor.

laws.title: Kyoto Temple Accessibility Improvements
laws.subtitle: Barrier-free access at heritage sites — complex balance
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's UNESCO World Heritage sites must balance accessibility obligations under the Barrier-Free Act with heritage conservation requirements that often prohibit ramps, lifts, or paving modifications. The Agency for Cultural Affairs and Ministry of Land have issued joint guidance allowing 'soft' accessibility measures (portable ramps, accessible entry points) without permanent structural modification. Several major temples (Kinkaku-ji, Ryoan-ji) have achieved partial accessibility certification.
laws.penalty: New public buildings adjacent to heritage sites must fully comply with Barrier-Free Act; heritage structures have modified standards
exceptions: Designated cultural properties exempt from structural modification requirements but must offer alternative accessible routes
laws.sourceLabel: MLIT — Barrier-Free Act Heritage Site Guidance

quiz.q: What approach does Japan recommend for making ancient temples accessible without damaging heritage fabric?
options: Modern glass lifts alongside historic buildings
Portable ramps and accessible entry points — 'soft' measures
Exempting all heritage sites from accessibility requirements
quiz.explanation: Japan's guidance recommends 'soft' accessibility measures — portable ramps, designated accessible entry points — that don't permanently modify the fabric of protected heritage buildings.

laws.title: Traditional Craftsperson Apprenticeship
laws.subtitle: Long apprenticeships governed by employment law
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's traditional craft industries — including lacquerware (蒔絵), Nishijin weaving, and Buddhist altar making — rely on multi-year apprenticeships. Under Japan's Labour Standards Act and Vocational Ability Development Promotion Act (職業能力開発促進法), apprenticeships must pay at least the minimum wage and provide standard labour protections. The Ministry of Economy designates 'Traditional Craftsperson' (伝統工芸士) qualifications recognising master-level skill after 12+ years practice.
laws.penalty: Apprenticeship agreements below minimum wage: back-pay + fines; exploitative apprenticeships: labour inspection action
exceptions: Brief unpaid try-out periods (max 3 days) before formal apprenticeship start

quiz.q: How many years of practice are required before a craftsperson can apply for Japan's 'Traditional Craftsperson' (伝統工芸士) certification?
quiz.explanation: Japan's Traditional Craftsperson (伝統工芸士) certification requires 12 or more years of practice in a designated traditional industry — reflecting the depth of skill required.

laws.title: Autumn Foliage Crowd Management
laws.subtitle: Kyoto manages 60 million koyo visitors annually
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's autumn foliage (紅葉, koyo) season — typically November–early December — attracts even larger crowds than cherry blossom season, exceeding 20 million visitors in November alone. Temple access is often timed and ticketed, with Kiyomizu-dera, Eikan-do, and Tofuku-ji implementing strict entry quotas during peak weekends. Road closures and traffic management around foliage hotspots are coordinated between Kyoto City and Kyoto Prefectural Police. Drone photography is prohibited in most temple precincts.
laws.penalty: Drone operation in prohibited zone (near temples): ¥500,000 fine under Civil Aeronautics Act; crowd zone violations: ordinance fines
exceptions: Licensed aerial photography with temple and city approval
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City Tourism Management — Koyo Season

quiz.q: What is 'koyo' (紅葉) in Japanese seasonal culture?
quiz.explanation: Koyo (紅葉) is the Japanese autumn foliage viewing tradition — celebrated when maple and ginkgo trees turn red and gold, typically in November in Kyoto.

laws.title: Kyoto Waste Reduction — Zero-Waste Temple Model
laws.subtitle: Kyoto temples lead Japan's zero-waste initiatives
laws.fullDescription: Several Kyoto temples — notably Ryoan-ji and Ginkaku-ji — have implemented zero-waste visitor management policies, refusing to provide single-use plastics and operating composting systems for organic waste. These are voluntary initiatives complementing Kyoto City's Waste Reduction Promotion Plan (ごみ半減プラン) which targets 50% waste reduction from 2000 levels by 2030. Kyoto City operates an unusual civic 'citizen consultation' system for waste policy decisions.
laws.penalty: Temple-specific no-plastic rules enforced through entry conditions (civil, not criminal); general Waste Management Act violations: standard fines
exceptions: Emergency use packaging
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City — Waste Reduction Promotion Plan

quiz.q: By what percentage does Kyoto City's waste reduction plan aim to cut waste from 2000 levels by 2030?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto City's Waste Reduction Promotion Plan (ごみ半減プラン) targets 50% waste reduction from 2000 levels by 2030 — one of Japan's most ambitious municipal targets.

laws.title: Antique and Art Theft — Kyoto's Temples at Risk
laws.subtitle: Temple art theft carries maximum cultural property penalties
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's thousands of temples and shrines hold extraordinary concentrations of cultural property — Buddhist statues, painted screens, tea utensils, and calligraphy. Theft of designated cultural properties carries enhanced penalties under the Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties beyond standard theft charges. Several high-profile thefts — including wooden Buddhist statues stolen from rural Kyoto temples — led to improved security funding. Police coordinate with Interpol for international art crime.
laws.penalty: Theft of designated cultural property: up to 10 years imprisonment; selling stolen cultural property: same + civil restitution
laws.sourceLabel: Agency for Cultural Affairs — Cultural Property Crime Response

quiz.q: What international organisation does Kyoto's police coordinate with to track stolen cultural property abroad?
quiz.explanation: Japan's police coordinate with Interpol's Works of Art unit to track culturally significant objects stolen from Kyoto temples that appear in overseas art markets.

laws.title: Kyoto Tourism Accommodation Tax
laws.subtitle: Japan's most sophisticated accommodation tax system
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City's accommodation tax (宿泊税), introduced in October 2018 and the first in Japan to graduate rates by nightly spend, charges: ¥200/night (rooms ¥20,000), ¥500/night (rooms ¥20,000–¥50,000), and ¥1,000/night (rooms over ¥50,000). Revenue funds tourism management infrastructure. Revenue exceeded ¥4 billion in FY2019 before COVID. Minpaku hosts must collect and remit the tax through their registration system.
laws.penalty: Accommodation operators not collecting/remitting tax: back-assessment + penalty surcharges up to 15%; systematic non-compliance: criminal referral
exceptions: Long-term residents (30+ day stays) exempt

quiz.q: What was Kyoto City's accommodation tax revenue in FY2019 (pre-COVID peak)?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto City's accommodation tax generated over ¥4 billion in FY2019 — significant revenue for tourism management before COVID devastated visitor numbers.

laws.title: Kyoto City Bus System — 100 Yen Loop Bus
laws.subtitle: Flat-fare tourist bus routes regulated by city
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City Bus and Kyoto Bus operate the city's primary public transport network. The tourist-friendly Raku Bus (洛バス) routes connect major temple areas with flat-fare or discount day pass options. Under the Road Transportation Act (道路運送法), bus routes and fares require Ministry of Land approval. Kyoto City provides operating subsidies to maintain unprofitable but socially necessary routes through residential areas with elderly populations.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed bus operation: up to 2 years imprisonment or ¥3,000,000 fine
exceptions: Private shuttle buses to specific venues (hotels, temples) with limited capacity

quiz.q: What is the name of Kyoto's special tourist bus routes connecting major heritage sites?
quiz.explanation: The Raku Bus (洛バス) are Kyoto City's dedicated tourist bus routes with easy-to-understand numbering connecting major temples and heritage sites.

laws.title: Nijo Castle World Heritage Management
laws.subtitle: Shogun's palace governed by strict preservation rules
laws.fullDescription: Nijo Castle (二条城), built by Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1603 as his Kyoto residence and listed as UNESCO World Heritage, is owned by Kyoto City and managed by the Nijo Castle Office. Entry fees and visitor management ensure conservation funding. The 'nightingale floors' (鶯張り) — designed to squeak when walked upon to detect intruders — are original and protected. Any commercial filming within the castle grounds requires Kyoto City approval and heritage authority review.
laws.penalty: Damage to Nijo Castle fabric: up to 5 years imprisonment; unauthorised commercial filming: ¥500,000 fine
exceptions: Educational documentary filming with prior approval
laws.sourceLabel: Nijo Castle — Kyoto City Management Office

quiz.q: What architectural security feature of Nijo Castle is both its most famous and most protected element?
options: Nightingale floors (鶯張り) designed to squeak when walked upon
quiz.explanation: Nijo Castle's nightingale floors (鶯張り) — deliberately engineered to squeak underfoot — served as an intrusion detection system and are now among Japan's most famous architectural features.

laws.title: Kyoto Restaurant Reservation Cancellation Policy
laws.subtitle: High-end restaurants enforcing cancellation deposits
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's high-end kaiseki restaurants — which require bookings weeks or months in advance — have faced a growing problem of no-shows and last-minute cancellations, particularly from international tourists. The Specified Commercial Transactions Act and civil contract law allow restaurants to charge cancellation fees if clearly stated in advance. Some establishments now take deposits (per person) credited to the meal. These policies, if disclosed, are legally enforceable civil contracts.
laws.penalty: No direct criminal penalty for cancellation; civil: restaurant can recover stated cancellation fee through court if necessary
exceptions: Force majeure (illness with documentation) typically waived by reputable establishments
laws.sourceLabel: Consumer Affairs Agency — Contract Cancellation Policy

quiz.q: What is 'kaiseki' (懐石) cuisine — the style served in Kyoto's most prestigious restaurants?
options: A type of ramen with multiple toppings
quiz.explanation: Kaiseki (懐石) is Japan's most refined multi-course cuisine — rooted in Kyoto's imperial and tea ceremony culture, using seasonal ingredients in artfully presented sequences of dishes.

laws.title: Imperial Household Law — Kyoto Imperial Palace
laws.subtitle: Imperial Palace sites subject to Imperial Household Agency rules
laws.fullDescription: The Kyoto Imperial Palace (京都御所) and Katsura Imperial Villa (桂離宮) are managed by the Imperial Household Agency (宮内庁) under the Imperial Household Agency Act. Public visits to the Palace grounds (opened without advance reservation since 2016) are subject to the Agency's conduct rules — no drones, no dogs, no running, no alcohol. Katsura Imperial Villa visits still require advance application. The Imperial Palace Site is Crown property — technically not Kyoto City's to regulate.
laws.penalty: Violating Imperial Household Agency site rules: removal + potential criminal trespass; damaging Crown property: civil and criminal liability
exceptions: Invited dignitaries and official state occasions
laws.sourceLabel: Imperial Household Agency — Site Visit Rules

quiz.q: Since what year can the public visit Kyoto Imperial Palace grounds without advance reservation?
quiz.explanation: The Kyoto Imperial Palace grounds opened to unreserved public access in 2016 — previously requiring advance application through the Imperial Household Agency.

laws.title: Lake Biwa Canal Water Rights
laws.subtitle: Kyoto's water supply from Lake Biwa governed by treaty
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City draws its water supply from Lake Biwa (琵琶湖), Japan's largest freshwater lake in Shiga Prefecture, via the Lake Biwa Canal (琵琶湖疏水) built 1885–1890. Water rights and quantity are governed by inter-prefectural agreements enforced under the River Act (河川法). Kyoto, Osaka, and Shiga coordinate management of the lake — Japan's largest drinking water reservoir. Pollution of the canal or lake causing disruption to Kyoto's water supply is a major environmental offence.
laws.penalty: Polluting Lake Biwa or its canal: up to 1 year imprisonment or ¥1,000,000 fine; criminal negligence causing water disruption: up to 5 years
exceptions: Permitted wastewater discharge within agreed limits from Shiga lakeside industry

quiz.q: What is the Lake Biwa Canal (琵琶湖疏水) — historically significant to Kyoto?
options: A decorative moat around Nijo Castle
A 19th-century canal bringing Lake Biwa water to supply Kyoto with drinking water and power
A drainage channel built by the Tokugawa Shogunate
quiz.explanation: The Lake Biwa Canal (琵琶湖疏水) built 1885–1890 was a landmark Meiji-era engineering project supplying Kyoto with drinking water, irrigation, and Japan's first hydroelectric power.

laws.title: Kyoto International Manga Museum
laws.subtitle: Public cultural facility subject to city governance rules
laws.fullDescription: The Kyoto International Manga Museum (京都国際マンガミュージアム), jointly operated by Kyoto City and Kyoto Seika University, houses 300,000+ manga volumes and is Japan's largest manga museum. Under Kyoto City's public facility regulations, the museum operates with bilingual staff, accessibility compliance, and content rating systems for adult manga areas. Manga is legally classified as a publication under the Publishing Act (出版法) — adult content restricted to designated areas.
laws.penalty: Allowing minors to access adult manga sections: administrative violation; theft from reading collection: theft charges
exceptions: Research access for qualified scholars

quiz.q: How many manga volumes does the Kyoto International Manga Museum hold?
quiz.explanation: The Kyoto International Manga Museum holds over 300,000 manga volumes — making it Japan's largest manga museum and a major resource for the medium's preservation.

laws.title: Drone Flight Restrictions — Temple Zones
laws.subtitle: Civil Aeronautics Act restricts drones near heritage sites
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Civil Aeronautics Act (航空法) prohibits drone flights within 150 metres of densely populated areas and requires approval for flights near airports, national infrastructure, and designated event areas. Kyoto additionally applies these restrictions near its UNESCO World Heritage temple compounds and historic districts. Many temple and shrine management organisations have posted their own drone prohibition notices that interact with trespass law if drones enter shrine airspace without consent.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed drone flight in restricted area: up to ¥500,000 fine; drone crash damaging cultural property: civil liability + potential criminal negligence
exceptions: MLIT-licensed aerial operators with advance approval from site managers
laws.sourceLabel: MLIT — Civil Aeronautics Act Drone Rules

quiz.q: What is the Civil Aeronautics Act restriction distance from densely populated areas for drone flights in Japan?
quiz.explanation: Japan's Civil Aeronautics Act prohibits drone flights within 150 metres of densely populated areas without MLIT approval — with additional restrictions near heritage sites and events.

laws.title: Temple Entry Fee Regulation
laws.subtitle: No legal cap on temple entry fees — market-driven
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's major temples charge entry fees ranging from ¥500 (many sites) to ¥3,000 (exclusive night-time light-up events). Unlike public parks, private religious institutions (寺院) are not regulated on pricing — they set fees freely. Some municipal-owned sites (Shinjuan sub-temple of Daitoku-ji) have local oversight. The trend toward higher fees and timed entry (particularly from 2023) reflects demand management by private religious corporations registered under the Religious Corporation Act (宗教法人法).
laws.penalty: N/A — entry fees are private commercial decisions; discriminatory pricing based on nationality may violate Anti-Discrimination guidelines
exceptions: Certain shrine inner sanctuaries (honden) are free as legally required by shrine management rules

quiz.q: Under what legal status do most of Kyoto's major temples and shrines operate?
options: Religious corporations (宗教法人) — private religious entities
quiz.explanation: Most of Kyoto's temples and shrines are registered as Religious Corporations (宗教法人) — private entities with significant legal autonomy, including the right to set their own entry fees.

laws.title: Kabuki Theatre — Minamiza Historic Venue
laws.subtitle: Japan's oldest kabuki theatre in Kyoto's Gion
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's Minamiza (南座) in Gion — dating to 1610 — is Japan's oldest kabuki theatre and a Registered Tangible Cultural Property (登録有形文化財). Kabuki (歌舞伎) performances are governed by the Japan Arts Council (日本芸術文化振興会) funding frameworks and the traditional iemoto (家元) hereditary master system of major families (Ichikawa, Nakamura, Onoe). Kabuki was inscribed as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2005. The December Kaomise (顔見世) in Kyoto is the kabuki world's most prestigious annual engagement.
laws.penalty: Damage to Minamiza as cultural property: up to 5 years; ticket fraud at major kabuki events: standard fraud penalties

quiz.q: When did Kabuki theatre receive UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage recognition?
quiz.explanation: Kabuki was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2005 — recognising it as a living traditional performing art.

laws.title: Traditional Medicine (Kampo) Practice
laws.subtitle: Kampo prescribed only by licensed medical doctors
laws.fullDescription: In Japan, unlike China, kampo (漢方) traditional herbal medicine can only be prescribed by licensed Western-trained medical doctors (医師) — there is no separate traditional medicine practitioner licence. Kyoto, as a centre of both Western and traditional medicine, has numerous hospital departments integrating kampo with modern treatment. Over 80% of Japanese physicians use kampo in their practice. Non-licensed kampo dispensing to patients claiming therapeutic benefit is illegal.
laws.penalty: Non-licensed prescription of kampo for medical conditions: up to 3 years imprisonment under Medical Practitioners Act
exceptions: Over-the-counter kampo preparations (general-use formulas) sold at pharmacies without prescription
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health — Traditional Medicine Integration

quiz.q: Who is legally authorised to prescribe kampo herbal medicine in Japan?
quiz.explanation: Only licensed Western-trained medical doctors (医師) can legally prescribe kampo in Japan — there is no separate traditional medicine licence category, unlike in China.

laws.title: Surrounding Mountain Forest Protection
laws.subtitle: Higashiyama and Kitayama forests are protected green belts
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's famous 'basin of mountains' (三方を山に囲まれた盆地) — the Higashiyama (東山), Kitayama (北山), and Nishiyama (西山) ranges surrounding the city on three sides — are protected under the Quasi-National Park designation and Kyoto Prefecture's Green Vision Plan. Logging, development, and recreational activities within designated protection zones require permits. These forests are both ecological corridors and the visual backdrop to Kyoto's heritage landscape.
laws.penalty: Unauthorised logging in protected forest zone: up to 1 year imprisonment or ¥1,000,000 fine
exceptions: Controlled cedar and hinoki cypress harvesting by licenced forestry operations in designated commercial zones
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Environment — Quasi-National Park Designations

quiz.q: How many mountain ranges surround Kyoto's basin, forming its characteristic enclosed landscape?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto sits in a basin surrounded by three mountain ranges: Higashiyama (east), Kitayama (north), and Nishiyama (west) — shaping the city's microclimate and visual character.

laws.title: Forgery of Cultural Property Documentation
laws.subtitle: Fake provenance documents for art and antiques
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's antique market attracts sophisticated fraud involving forged provenance documents (来歴書), attribution seals (印), and certificates of authenticity for traditional art. Such forgeries are prosecuted under Penal Code document forgery provisions (私文書偽造, up to 5 years) and fraud charges if used to secure payment. The Japanese Art and Antique Dealers Association (全国美術商連合会) maintains standards and blacklists known fraudsters. Interpol Art Crime databases include Kyoto-linked cases.
laws.penalty: Document forgery: up to 5 years imprisonment; fraud using forged documents: up to 10 years

quiz.q: What Japanese legal term covers the crime of forging private documents like art provenance certificates?
options: Shibunso gizo (私文書偽造, private document forgery)
quiz.explanation: Shibunso gizo (私文書偽造) — private document forgery — is the Penal Code offence covering fake art provenance documents, carrying up to 5 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Kurama and Kibune Mountain Trail Rules
laws.subtitle: Sacred mountain trails have conduct requirements
laws.fullDescription: Kurama-dera (鞍馬寺) and Kibune Jinja (貴船神社) in the mountains north of Kyoto operate their hiking trails under both property law and religious site management rules. Kurama-dera charges a 'nature preservation fee' (¥300) for mountain access. Hunting is prohibited — the mountains are part of a wildlife sanctuary. Camping and fire-making are banned. The trails close at dusk. Social media viral content of nighttime trail visits has prompted increased enforcement.
laws.penalty: Nighttime trespass on Kurama-dera property: removal and potential criminal trespass; fire-making: up to ¥300,000 fine
exceptions: Temple-organised special dawn events

quiz.q: What fee does Kurama-dera charge for hiking its mountain trails — framed as a preservation contribution?
quiz.explanation: Kurama-dera charges a ¥300 'nature preservation fee' (愛山費) for access to its mountain trails — reinvested in trail maintenance and wildlife protection.

laws.title: Kyoto University IPS Cell Patent Framework
laws.subtitle: University intellectual property governed by University IP Policy
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto University's iPS cell technology (induced pluripotent stem cells), developed by Prof. Shinya Yamanaka (2006, Nobel 2012), generated a complex intellectual property situation: KyotoUniversity licensed the technology globally while defending core patents against challenges from foreign universities. The Japanese government's Universities IP Act (大学知的財産法) and Technology Transfer Organisation (TLO) system govern how universities patent and commercialise research. KU holds over 200 iPS-related patents.
laws.penalty: Infringement of KU iPS patents: civil damages; deliberate infringement: criminal provisions under Patent Act (最大10年)
exceptions: Research use exemption allows academic use without licence

quiz.q: In what year did Shinya Yamanaka at Kyoto University first publish his iPS cell research?
quiz.explanation: Yamanaka's landmark paper on induced pluripotent stem cells was published in 2006 — he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2012.

laws.title: Obon Festival Management — Daimonji
laws.subtitle: Five mountain bonfires for Gozan no Okuribi regulated
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's Gozan no Okuribi (五山の送り火, August 16) — five giant bonfires in kanji shapes on surrounding mountains sending off ancestral spirits — is managed by five separate neighbourhood preservation organisations under Kyoto City fire safety oversight. The Fire Service Act governs the lighting permits, fuel quantities, and volunteer fire brigade standby. Viewing spots fill to capacity; the city manages crowd flow along the Kamo River. Unauthorised viewing from mountain trails creates safety risks.
laws.penalty: Trespassing on bonfire mountains during the event: criminal trespass; unauthorized ignition of mountain bonfires: arson charges
exceptions: Authorised neighbourhood preservation society members
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City — Gozan no Okuribi Management

quiz.q: When is Kyoto's Gozan no Okuribi (五山の送り火) mountain bonfire festival held?
quiz.explanation: Gozan no Okuribi is held on August 16, the final night of the Obon festival — when giant bonfires on Kyoto's five surrounding mountains send ancestral spirits back to the afterlife.

laws.title: Kyoto International Community — CIR Programme
laws.subtitle: JET Programme coordinators in Kyoto schools
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City participates in Japan's JET Programme (Japan Exchange and Teaching Programme), placing Coordinators for International Relations (CIR) and Assistant Language Teachers (ALT) in schools and government offices. JET participants are on working visas with specific conditions — tied to their host institution. Kyoto's international student population additionally benefits from the Student Exchange promotion, with Kyoto University hosting over 3,000 international students.
laws.penalty: JET participants violating visa conditions (working outside placement): deportation risk; overstaying: criminal charges
exceptions: JET participants may do limited translation/interpreting work if approved by host

quiz.q: What does CIR stand for in the JET Programme context?
quiz.explanation: CIR stands for Coordinator for International Relations — JET Programme participants placed in government offices and international relations roles, distinct from ALT (Assistant Language Teacher) placements.

laws.title: Tax-Free Shopping for Foreign Tourists
laws.subtitle: Consumption tax refund at registered retailers
laws.fullDescription: Foreign tourists visiting Japan may purchase goods tax-free (消費税免税) at registered retailers by presenting a passport. The consumption tax (消費税, currently 10%) is exempted on general goods purchased over ¥5,000 in one transaction. Kyoto's dense retail and craft districts — Shijo-dori department stores, Nishiki Market, temple souvenir shops — are popular for tax-free shopping. Goods must leave Japan within 30 days and not be used in Japan.
laws.penalty: Using tax-free purchased goods in Japan (not exporting): back-assessment of consumption tax + surcharge; fraudulent use of another's passport for tax-free: fraud charges
exceptions: Consumables (food, cosmetics) have separate lower threshold and must be packed and sealed

quiz.q: What is the minimum purchase amount for a single transaction to qualify for tax-free shopping in Japan?
quiz.explanation: Foreign tourists must spend at least ¥5,000 in a single transaction at a registered retailer to qualify for tax-free shopping in Japan.

laws.title: Cycle Tourism Programme — Kyoto
laws.subtitle: Rental bike network regulated for tourist safety
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City operates and licences a network of bicycle rental stations (docomo bike share) for tourists exploring the city between temple areas. Cyclists must comply with Road Traffic Act provisions: ride on the left, use lights at night, no more than two abreast. Cycling on pedestrian footpaths (人道) is generally prohibited for adults except on designated paths — violations in Gion's narrow streets have caused pedestrian injuries. Some routes (Philosopher's Walk) are cycling-friendly; temple precincts are always dismount zones.
laws.penalty: Cycling on prohibited footpaths: ¥20,000 fine; riding without lights at night: ¥50,000 fine
exceptions: Designated cycling paths on temple approaches where permitted

quiz.q: What is Kyoto's 'Philosopher's Walk' (哲学の道) — one of the city's most famous cycling and walking routes?
options: A mountain hiking trail above Higashiyama
A canal-side path through northern Higashiyama connecting Nanzen-ji to Ginkaku-ji
A boulevard through central Kyoto lined with philosophy faculty buildings
An underground walking route connecting temple museums
quiz.explanation: The Philosopher's Walk (哲学の道) is a picturesque canal-side path in northern Higashiyama, named after philosopher Nishida Kitaro who meditated along it — famous for cherry blossoms.

laws.title: Cultural Property Illegal Export — International Cases
laws.subtitle: Kyoto objects appearing in foreign auctions trigger investigations
laws.fullDescription: Japanese police and the Agency for Cultural Affairs work with Interpol and Christie's/Sotheby's to identify Kyoto cultural properties appearing in foreign auction markets without proper export documentation. Japan joined the 1970 UNESCO Convention on stolen cultural property. Notable cases include Buddhist statues stolen from rural Kyoto reaching European art markets. UNIDROIT Convention obligations mean Japan can seek return of stolen objects from contracting states.
laws.penalty: Smuggling cultural property out of Japan: up to 5 years + ¥5,000,000 fine; receiving stolen cultural property: up to 10 years
exceptions: Objects legally exported with cultural authority permits before new restrictions
laws.sourceLabel: Agency for Cultural Affairs — International Cultural Property Recovery

quiz.q: Which international convention on cultural property did Japan join, enabling recovery of stolen objects from other member states?
quiz.explanation: Japan acceded to both the 1970 UNESCO Convention and UNIDROIT Convention on stolen cultural property — enabling legal return of stolen objects appearing in international markets.

laws.title: Dark Sky Protection — Observatory Hill
laws.subtitle: Kyoto limits light pollution near Observatory
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's Kwasan Observatory (花山天文台, operated by Kyoto University since 1929) and Hida Observatory have benefited from Kyoto's strict signage and lighting restrictions, which incidentally reduce light pollution. Kyoto City's Landscape Policy limits rooftop illumination and requires outdoor lighting to be directed downward. While not specifically a 'dark sky ordinance,' the combination of height limits, sign restrictions, and lighting rules has preserved darker skies than most Japanese cities.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant outdoor lighting (directed upward): landscape ordinance fines up to ¥300,000
exceptions: Temporary event lighting with approval
Safety required lighting

quiz.q: Since what year has Kyoto University operated its Kwasan Observatory on a Kyoto hillside?
quiz.explanation: Kwasan Observatory (花山天文台) has been operated by Kyoto University since 1929 — benefiting from the city's strict lighting restrictions that incidentally limit light pollution.

laws.title: Kyoto Station Area Management
laws.subtitle: Kyoto Station as infrastructure hub under special rules
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto Station (京都駅) — a major JR hub on the Tokaido Shinkansen, designed by Hiroshi Hara (1997) — is partly regulated under Airport-level security concepts despite being a rail terminal. JR West manages the station as a commercial complex. The 15-floor building houses a department store, hotels, cinema, and 75,000 daily passengers. Large-group gathering and demonstration within the station concourse require station management approval. The station's iconic 'Space Frame' glass atrium is a designated modern architectural landmark.
laws.penalty: Unauthorised commercial activities in station: removal; demonstration without approval: station exclusion + potential public nuisance ordinance application
exceptions: Traditional religious and charity collections with management permission

quiz.q: Who designed Kyoto Station's distinctive 1997 modern glass-and-steel building?
quiz.explanation: Hiroshi Hara designed Kyoto Station's bold 1997 building — controversial at the time for its modern aesthetic in a historic city, but now celebrated as a landmark.

laws.title: Kyoto City LGBT Support Declaration
laws.subtitle: Partnership certificates available since 2020
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City introduced its Diversity Partner Certificate (パートナーシップ認定制度) in September 2020. The certificate provides recognition for same-sex couples in city services, public housing applications, and hospital visitings. Kyoto University became one of Japan's first national universities to provide housing and facility access to same-sex student couples in 2017. Kyoto Prefecture followed with its own scheme in 2023.
laws.penalty: N/A — rights-granting provision
exceptions: National marriage law unchanged — certificates confer administrative recognition only

quiz.q: When did Kyoto City introduce its same-sex partnership certificate scheme?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto City introduced its Diversity Partner Certificate (パートナーシップ認定制度) in September 2020, providing administrative recognition for same-sex couples.

laws.title: Nishiki-in and Kyoto Gosho Buffer Zone
laws.subtitle: Development around Imperial Palace strictly controlled
laws.fullDescription: The area surrounding Kyoto Gosho (Imperial Palace) is subject to a buffer zone under the Kyoto Urban Planning Law specifying low-rise, traditional-scale development. The Imperial Household Agency's management of the grounds is coordinated with Kyoto City's planning for surrounding Nakagyo Ward. Building height limits of 10–15 metres apply in the buffer; parking structures and commercial buildings face additional restrictions to preserve the Palace's visual setting.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant development in buffer zone: planning refusal + potential demolition order
exceptions: Traditional Japanese-style commercial buildings within height limits
laws.sourceLabel: Kyoto City Urban Planning — Imperial Palace Buffer Zone

quiz.q: In which ward of Kyoto is the Imperial Palace (Kyoto Gosho) located?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto Gosho (Imperial Palace) is located in Nakagyo Ward (中京区) — surrounded by a preserved buffer zone of low-rise traditional-scale development.

laws.title: Souvenir Authenticity — Kyoto Craft Certification
laws.subtitle: Kyoto Brand certification for genuine local crafts
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City operates the 'Kyoto Brand' (京都ブランド) certification system for genuine locally produced crafts and food products. Products are vetted for production location, technique, and material authenticity. Uncertified products using misleading 'Kyoto-style' or 'made in Kyoto' language when produced elsewhere may violate the Unfair Competition Prevention Act's false origin provisions. Tourist shops in Gion and Arashiyama have been investigated for selling China-manufactured goods with Kyoto presentation.
laws.penalty: False origin labelling: up to 5 years imprisonment or ¥5,000,000 fine under Unfair Competition Prevention Act
exceptions: 'Kyoto-style' design without false origin claim is generally permitted

quiz.q: What legal protection prevents manufacturers from falsely claiming products are 'made in Kyoto' when they are not?
options: Unfair Competition Prevention Act (不正競争防止法)
quiz.explanation: Japan's Unfair Competition Prevention Act (不正競争防止法) prohibits false origin claims — protecting Kyoto's authentic craft industry from copycat products falsely marketed as locally made.

laws.title: Kyoto Basin Flooding Risk Management
laws.subtitle: Kamo River flood control under River Act
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto's basin geography makes it vulnerable to flash flooding when typhoons stall over Kinki. The Kamo River (鴨川) and Katsura River (桂川) are managed under the River Act (河川法) with flood control structures including the Kamo River weir system. Residents in designated flood risk zones must register in evacuation plans. The 2021 Kyoto flood insurance programme covers 85% of flood-prone district residents — one of Japan's highest participation rates.
laws.penalty: Development blocking natural flood channels: demolition orders; failure to evacuate during official warning: fines under Disaster Countermeasures Act
exceptions: Heritage structures in flood zones receive modified flood protection without displacement

quiz.q: Kyoto's basin geography makes it vulnerable to flooding from which natural phenomenon?
options: Typhoons stalling over the Kinki region
Tsunami from Osaka Bay via river channels
Groundwater flooding from the Kyoto aquifer
quiz.explanation: Kyoto's enclosed basin geography concentrates rainfall when typhoons stall over the Kinki region — the Kamo and Katsura rivers can rise rapidly, threatening low-lying districts.

laws.title: Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University — Kyoto Link
laws.subtitle: Ritsumeikan system bridges Kyoto and international campuses
laws.fullDescription: Ritsumeikan University, founded in Kyoto in 1900, operates a network including its international campus Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University (APU) in Beppu. Under Japan's University Act, all Ritsumeikan campuses share accreditation through a single university corporation (学校法人). APU — with over 50% international students — is subject to immigration rules, academic freedom protections, and financial sustainability audits by the Ministry of Education. Kyoto's Ritsumeikan campus hosts Japan's largest repository of peace education research.
laws.penalty: University accreditation fraud: up to ¥1,000,000 fine + closure order; degree fraud: criminal fraud charges
exceptions: Research programmes may have different disclosure requirements from undergraduate courses

quiz.q: What percentage of students at Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University (APU) are international?
quiz.explanation: APU (Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University) in Beppu has over 50% international students — making it Japan's most internationally diverse university campus.

laws.title: Stimulant Drug Enforcement — Kyoto University Context
laws.subtitle: Drug enforcement in Japan's academic capital
