laws.fullDescription: Kyoto Prefecture Police's narcotics division enforces stimulant drug laws in the densely student-populated areas of Kyoto — particularly around Kyoto University (Yoshida Campus), Doshisha (Imadegawa), and Ritsumeikan (Kinugasa). Campus incidents involving stimulants (primarily methamphetamine and now MDMA) have prompted police-university cooperation programmes. Kyoto University's reputation for academic freedom extends to tolerance of unconventional student culture, but drug use receives no institutional protection.
laws.penalty: Methamphetamine possession: up to 10 years; MDMA possession: up to 3 years; trafficking: up to life (stimulants) or 7 years (MDMA)

quiz.q: What recreational drug has seen increased enforcement action at Kyoto university areas beyond traditional methamphetamine?
quiz.explanation: MDMA use has grown among Japanese university students, prompting increased enforcement near Kyoto's university campuses — possession carries up to 3 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Kyoto Convention Bureau — Event Licensing
laws.subtitle: International conferences require city and police coordination
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto is Japan's premier international conference city (ranked by number of international meetings hosted). Large international events at venues including the Kyoto International Conference Centre (国立京都国際会館) require coordination with the Kyoto Convention Bureau, Fire Department, and Prefectural Police. Events with foreign government representatives trigger diplomatic protection protocols. The Conference Centre — Japan's first purpose-built international conference facility (1966) — is a Registered Cultural Property.
laws.penalty: Events exceeding capacity without fire safety clearance: closure orders; illegal commercial event at cultural venue: civil breach of contract
exceptions: Academic conferences with established city relationships have streamlined permitting

quiz.q: When did Kyoto International Conference Centre open as Japan's first dedicated international conference venue?
quiz.explanation: Kyoto International Conference Centre opened in 1966 as Japan's first purpose-built international conference facility — hosting events including the 1997 Kyoto Protocol signing.

laws.title: Fushimi Inari Fox Messenger Statues Protection
laws.subtitle: Kitsune statues at shrines are religious property
laws.fullDescription: Fushimi Inari Taisha's thousands of stone fox (kitsune, 狐) messenger statues — positioned throughout its 10,000-torii mountain trail — are the private religious property of the shrine corporation. Touching, climbing, or moving the statues is prohibited. Vandalism has occurred from international tourists unfamiliar with their religious significance. The shrine has installed cameras and security patrols. Deliberate damage constitutes criminal property damage of religious property, which carries enhanced social stigma.
laws.penalty: Damage to shrine religious objects: criminal property damage up to 3 years + civil restoration cost; theft: up to 10 years
exceptions: Shrine priests performing ritual maintenance

quiz.q: What animal messenger is associated with Inari (稲荷) shrines like Fushimi Inari Taisha?
quiz.explanation: The fox (kitsune, 狐) is the divine messenger of Inari — the Shinto deity of rice, agriculture, and prosperity. Fushimi Inari's thousands of stone foxes represent messengers between the human and divine realms.

laws.title: Wisteria and Seasonal Garden Rules
laws.subtitle: Private gardens opened seasonally under visitor agreements
laws.fullDescription: Several famous Kyoto gardens — Byodoin (平等院) wisteria, Daikaku-ji (大覚寺) autumnal ponds, and various sub-temple gardens — open to public during specific seasons on a ticketed, limited-entry basis. Entry is governed by private property consent agreements. Photography for personal use is generally permitted but commercial photography requires written consent. Drones are universally prohibited. Touching plants, picking flowers, or entering restricted garden areas breaches these private entry agreements.
laws.penalty: Property damage to private garden (picking flowers, damaging trees): civil liability + potential criminal property damage; commercial photo without consent: copyright/contract breach
exceptions: Guided tours with pre-arranged commercial photography licences

quiz.q: What is Byodoin (平等院) in Kyoto most famous for featuring on Japanese currency?
options: The Phoenix Hall (鳳凰堂) appearing on the ¥10 coin
quiz.explanation: Byodoin's Phoenix Hall (鳳凰堂) in Uji, Kyoto appears on Japan's ¥10 coin — making it one of the country's most recognised architectural landmarks.

laws.title: Kyoto Discrimination Prohibition Guidelines
laws.subtitle: Kyoto has strong local anti-discrimination framework
laws.fullDescription: Kyoto City has adopted a Hate Speech Countermeasures Ordinance (ヘイトスピーチ対策) following high-profile incidents in the Fushimi/Uji area targeting the Korean minority community. Kyoto City also published an anti-discrimination guidance framework covering service denial to foreigners, disability discrimination, and gender discrimination. While not all provisions carry direct criminal penalties, they give grounds for civil action and administrative investigation under national and local law frameworks.
laws.penalty: Hate speech with criminal elements (threats, assault): criminal charges; civil discrimination in service provision: civil tort liability; administrative guidance for systematic discrimination

quiz.q: What community in Kyoto has been the target of hate speech incidents that prompted the city's anti-discrimination ordinance?
quiz.explanation: High-profile hate speech incidents targeting Kyoto's Zainichi Korean community — particularly around Uji City — prompted Kyoto to adopt its Hate Speech Countermeasures Ordinance.

laws.title: Kyoto Cultural Property Digital Archive Law
laws.subtitle: Digitalisation of cultural properties subject to copyright and access rules
laws.fullDescription: Japan's Cultural Property Protection Law was amended to facilitate digital archiving of cultural properties. Kyoto City and the national Agency for Cultural Affairs operate digital repositories of temple treasures, historical maps, and intangible heritage recordings. Under the Copyright Act, works over 70 years old whose authors are dead enter public domain, but modern photographs and 3D scans of cultural properties may be subject to new copyright claims. The Kyoto Institute of Technology's 3D scanning of heritage objects has required careful IP framework development.
laws.penalty: Unauthorised commercial use of copyrighted heritage documentation: up to 10 years imprisonment or ¥10,000,000 fine
exceptions: Non-commercial educational and research use of public domain heritage material
laws.sourceLabel: Agency for Cultural Affairs — Cultural Property Digital Archive

quiz.q: How long after an author's death do works enter the public domain in Japan?
quiz.explanation: Japan extended its copyright term from 50 to 70 years post-author death in 2018, aligning with EU and US standards — affecting the public domain status of many historical cultural works.
